## Task 1 - Slate Health Check {#sec-task-1}

This is a high-level overview of the financial health and composition of the studios past slate. The code for preparing the data for this task can be found below. Note that we are filtering out any movie with a recorded budget less than 1000 USD from the dataset. This is because most film budgets in the dataset are recorded in actual dollars, but budgets below 1,000 appear to use inconsistent units, with some recorded in hundreds of thousands or millions of dollars. For example, *Escape from Tomorrow* has a recorded budget of 650 in the dataset. The film's actual reported budget was $650,000. Rather than attempting to source new budget data for each of the films with a reported budget less than 1000 dollars, which may be inconsistent with the data we already have, we are choosing to discard these unrealistic budgets. Note that in @tbl-slate-specifics-summary this leaves the lowest non-franchise film budget as $7,000; we can trace this back to *Primer*, a 2004 sci-fi film that really was shot on a $7,000 budget!

We have the same issues with revenue for some movies; for example *Dreaming of Joseph Lees* has a reported revenue of 7 in the dataset, against a budget of 2,000,000. Most internet sources seem to suggest the actual revenue for the film was somewhere between 7,000 to 13,000 dollars. Obviously if the production budget really was in the millions of dollars, this represents a tremendous failure. 

However, in terms of total financial impact to the studio, a film that costs $2,000,000 and doesn't make that back doesn't even register. The type of flops we want to make sure we have recorded are movies like *Cutthroat Island*, which had revenue of ~$10m against a budget of ~$98m. As such, we feel comfortable cutting movies with unrealistically low revenues out of the dataset as well. 

This cleaning should leave us with only films where we can be reasonably certain the figures we have are accurate, or at least have the right order of magnitude.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true

target_cols <- c("title", "budget", "roi", "franchise_status", "primary_genre", "release_year", "cast_size")
task_1_data <- data |>
  filter(
    budget >= 1000, # filtering out movies with a recorded budget below 1000 USD
    revenue >= 1000
  ) |> 
  dplyr::select(all_of(target_cols)) |> 
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) na_if(x, 0))) |> 
  mutate(
    franchise_status = factor(franchise_status)
  )
```

### Summary of data

@tbl-slate-overall-summary provides overall summary statistics for the budgets of films in our dataset, grouped by whether or not they were part of a franchise.


::: {#nte-franchise-coding .callout-note}

## Coding for Original vs Franchise

First films in a franchise are labelled as "Original" rather than as part of a franchise, and are therefore included in the data for the "Original" variable (see @tbl-slate-specifics-summary, where *Paranormal Activity* is the Original film with the best ROI, and *Paranormal Activity 2* is the Franchise film with the best ROI.)

Additionally, some films that are clearly part of a franchise are not labelled as such in the dataset; all 4 Pirates of the Caribbean movies are labelled as Original movies, for example.

As such, the below figures should be taken as indicative of overall trends only, not treated as absolute truths.

:::


```{r}
#| label: tbl-slate-overall-summary
#| tbl-cap: Summary statistics for the studio's historical slate

task_1_data |> 
  group_by(franchise_status) |> 
  summarise(
    `Number of movies` = as.character(n()),
    `Most Common Genre` = paste0(
      names(which.max(table(primary_genre))),
      " (n = ",
      max(table(primary_genre)),
      ")"
    ),
    `Mean Production Budget (USD millions)` = as.character(
      round(mean(budget, na.rm = TRUE) / 1e6, 2)
    ),
    `Median Production Budget (USD millions)` = as.character(
      round(median(budget, na.rm = TRUE) / 1e6, 2)
    ),
    `Production Budget Standard Deviation (USD millions)` = as.character(
      round(sd(budget, na.rm = TRUE) / 1e6, 2)
    ),
    `Mean Return on Investment (ROI)` = as.character(
      round(mean(roi, na.rm = TRUE), 2)
    ),
    `Median ROI` = as.character(
      round(median(roi, na.rm = TRUE), 2)
    ),
    `ROI Standard Deviation` = as.character(
      round(sd(roi, na.rm = TRUE), 2)
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |> 

  # pivoting long and then wide to get Franchise and Original to be our variable names
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -franchise_status,
    names_to = "Statistic",
    values_to = "Value"
  ) |> 
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = franchise_status,
    values_from = Value
  ) |> 
  gt() |> 
  cols_align(
    align = "left",
    columns = Statistic
  ) |> 
  cols_align(
    align = "center",
    columns = c(Original, Franchise)
  )
```

@tbl-slate-specifics-summary contains more specific information i.e. maximum and minimum costs, best and worst ROIs, etc. Movie title is presented in italics alongside the figures.

### Budget and ROI plots

```{r}
#| label: fig-basic-boxplots
#| fig-cap: Boxplots showing distribution of budgets and Return on Investment (Revenue divided by Budget) for Original vs Franchise films
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-subcap: 
#| - Budget
#| - ROI; dashed red line is at ROI = 1 i.e. films above the line made a profit, films below lost money

task_1_data |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = franchise_status, y = budget/1e6, fill = franchise_status)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(
    x = "Film Status",
    y = "Film budget (USD millions)"
  ) +
  theme_bw()

task_1_data |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = franchise_status, y = roi, fill = franchise_status)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_y_continuous(
    trans = transform_pseudo_log() # using a function from the scales package to compress the y axis, as we have some extreme outliers in Original movies for ROI
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Film Status",
    y = "Return on Investment (Revenue/Budget)"
  ) +

```

From the plots in @fig-basic-boxplots, and given what we know about how films are coded (@nte-franchise-coding), we can draw some conclusions from the above plots:

1. Sequels are generally more expensive to make than original films
2. Sequels are generally a safer bet than original films; they have a higher ROI on average, and are less likely to fall below an ROI of 1 (meaning they generally at least make their money back)
3. Original films have a higher ceiling for ROI
    - This is probably at least somewhat a function of point 1
    - Original movies are often made for smaller amounts, and if an original movie is a surprise hit and does reasonably well at the box office on a small budget, ROI will look enormous

But what about genre? Does that have an effect on movie finances?

### Slate composition over time

As we saw in @fig-genre-plots, there are a lot of genres in our dataset, many of which don't have many films at all. In order to explore shifts in slate composition, we just want to look at our top genres so the plot doesn't become a tangled mess. The number of genres chosen was eyeballed from what looked relevant in the plots above (landed on 5), and those genres are:

- Action
- Adventure
- Comedy
- Drama
- Horror

Worth noting is that although we have some data from 2015 on, it is not complete data and is therefore not included in @fig-genre-line-chart. It is unclear if the data we have from 2014 is fully complete, and some of the drops in numbers seen for genres like Adventure and Drama should therefore be taken with a grain of salt.

```{r}
#| label: fig-genre-line-chart
#| fig-cap: Line chart showing trend in genre releases over time; top 5 genres by total count are highlighted; film releases have been aggregated into 5 year blocks to make trends more visible

NUMBER_OF_GENRES <- 5

top_genres <- task_1_data |> 
  filter(!is.na(primary_genre), primary_genre != "") |> 
  count(primary_genre, sort = TRUE) |> 
  slice_max(n, n = NUMBER_OF_GENRES) |> 
  pull(primary_genre)

genre_counts <- task_1_data |> 
  filter(
    primary_genre != "",
    release_year < 2015 # we have very limited data from 2015 on, which skews the plot awkwardly and makes trends harder to see
  ) |> 
  mutate(year_period = (release_year %/% 5) * 5) |> 
  count(year_period, primary_genre, name = "n")

ggplot(genre_counts, aes(x = year_period, y = n, group = primary_genre)) +
  geom_line(
    data = filter(genre_counts, !primary_genre %in% top_genres),
    colour = "grey",
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = filter(genre_counts, primary_genre %in% top_genres),
    aes(colour = primary_genre),
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Year of release",
    y = "Number of films",
    colour = "Primary genre"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

## Task 2

Budget data are often skewed, and the median is often more meaningful than the mean when describing a budget for typical franchise and original categories. 
Here I will be using bootstraping to find 95% interval estimate for the difference in median budget between the two groups. As bootstraping simulates repeated samples from a population like the csv provided here, it can help us to describe the uncertainity in the data.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-budget-status-summary

clean_data_t2 <- data |>
  dplyr::select(franchise_status,budget) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) na_if(x, 0))) |> 
  mutate(
    franchise_status = factor(franchise_status)
  ) |> 
  filter(!is.na(franchise_status), !is.na(budget))


t2_sum_table <- clean_data_t2 |> 
  group_by(franchise_status) |> 
  summarise(
    observations = n(),
    median = median(budget, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd = sd(budget, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

```

```{r}
point_est_t2 <- t2_sum_table$median[t2_sum_table$franchise_status == "Franchise"] - t2_sum_table$median[t2_sum_table$franchise_status == "Original"]
```

As interpreted from the @fig-basic-boxplots (a) and the @tbl-budget-status-summary, the 'original' franchise status have the lower median which shows that the production budgets are biased towards the 'franchise' category. To confirm this we will use bootstraping. The point estimate of the data is `{r} point_est_t2` which we will use to confirm if bootstarped estimate is similar or not. If yes, then the budget allocation is truely are leaned towards 'franchise' category.

```{r}

perform_bootstrap <- function() {
  
  one_boot <- clean_data_t2 |> 
    group_by(franchise_status) |> 
    slice_sample(prop = 1, replace = TRUE)
  
  one_result <- one_boot |> 
    summarise(med_budget = median(budget), .groups = "drop") |> 
    summarise(
      diff_median = med_budget[franchise_status == "Franchise"] - 
                    med_budget[franchise_status == "Original"]
    )
  
  return(one_result)
}

set.seed(36)

bootstrap_results <- map_dfr(
  .x = 1:5000,
  .f = ~ perform_bootstrap()
)

ci_95 <- quantile(bootstrap_results$diff_median, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
```

The percentile bootstrap confidence interval of the data is `{r} ci_95[1]` and `{r} ci_95[2]`. The interval suggests that the population median difference is plausible between these values based on the data and bootstrap method.

### Does it verify leadership concern?

```{r}
bootstrap_results |>  
  ggplot(aes(x = diff_median)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = point_est_t2)+
  geom_vline(xintercept = ci_95[1], linetype = "dashed")+
  geom_vline(xintercept = ci_95[2], linetype = "dashed")+
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Bootstrap Distribution: Difference in Median Budgets",
    subtitle = "Franchise Median - Original Median (Simple line = observed, Dashed = 95% CI)",
    x = "Difference in Median Budget (USD)",
    y = "Frequency"
  )
```

This shows that the median difference is well above zero and similar to the point estimate which supports the concerns of the leadership of franchise slate absorbing much larger budgets than original slate.
   
Additionally from @sec-task-1 @fig-basic-boxplots, we can interpret that the originals have higher number of outliers that drastically increases the profits of the production houses. However, the overall ROI in origianls is low.

### Summary

The median is the best way to summarise the budget data as they are always right skewed and using mean won't provide any acceptable information. We needed to know about the difference in median of the two facets of franchise status to confirm the concern of the leadership about the baised budget allocation towards franchises. By boostraping the median difference of the `franchise_status` categories and creating a histogram of it showed that the median difference is well above zero (near 18 Million) which confirms the concern about budget allocations. 

However, ss stated in @sec-task-1, the sequels are much expensive to make than the originals and they have higher ROI than the originals, due to this reason the production houses are more inclined towards producing sequals as they have much better chance of creating profits than the originals. But from @sec-task-1 @fig-basic-boxplots, we can interpret that the originals have higher number of outliers that drastically increases the profits of the production houses. However, the overall ROI in origianls is low.

### Advice
The advice to the leadership is to focus on original movies that have high potential such as the genre that have the most profitable originals and gradually increase the budget allocation for them and compare the profits generated by both categories simultaniously and changing or refining the new original story selection strategy, find a optimised allocation stratergy that maximises the profits for the company. 

Choosing more originals carefully and strategically, provides more room for higher profits and gradually trying and testing original category in different genre and creating an optimal budget allocation for movies can increase the profits with a high margin. 

## Task 3
### Part 1: Production Budget Modelling
With the goal to construct a model that models an appropriate movie budget distribution, a competitor budget analysis was conducted as a credible reference point in line with industry standards. This was performed by sampling the budgeting model from Universal Pictures Studios, which is a direct industry competitor, and fitting a realistic probability model for Meridian to follow. 

```{r, warning = FALSE}
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-align: center
#Check distribution
universal <- data |> 
  filter(primary_company == "Universal Pictures" & budget > 0) |> 
  mutate(budget = budget/1e6  )

ggplot(universal, aes(x = budget,)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 10)+
  labs(title = "Distribution of Universal Pictures Film Budgets")

```

After data processing, the budget distribution is right skewed and only contain positive values. Therefore, exponential, Gamma, Log normal and  Weibull distribution can be selected for model evaluation. 

```{r, warning = FALSE}
#Fit plot
budget_normal <- fitdistr(
  universal$budget,
  densfun = "normal"
)


budget_exp <- fitdistr(
  universal$budget,
  densfun = "exponential"
)

budget_gamma <- fitdistr(
  universal$budget,
  densfun = "gamma"
)

budget_weibull <- fitdistr(
  universal$budget,
  densfun = "weibull"
)

budget_lognormal <- fitdistr(
  universal$budget,
  densfun = "lognormal"
)

```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-align: center
#qqplot
qq_normal <- 
  ggplot(universal, aes(sample = budget)) +
  stat_qq(
    distribution = qnorm,
    dparams = as.list(budget_normal$estimate)
  ) +
  stat_qq_line(
    distribution = qnorm,
    dparams = as.list(budget_normal$estimate)
  ) +
  labs(title = "Normal")

qq_exponential <- 
  ggplot(universal, aes(sample = budget)) +
  stat_qq(
    distribution = qexp,
    dparams = as.list(budget_exp$estimate)
  ) +
  stat_qq_line(
    distribution = qexp,
    dparams = as.list(budget_exp$estimate)
  ) +
  labs(title = "Exponential")

qq_gamma <- 
  ggplot(universal, aes(sample = budget)) +
  stat_qq(
    distribution = qgamma,
    dparams = as.list(budget_gamma$estimate)
  ) +
  stat_qq_line(
    distribution = qgamma,
    dparams = as.list(budget_gamma$estimate)
  ) +
  labs(title = "Gamma")

qq_weibull <- 
  ggplot(universal, aes(sample = budget)) +
  stat_qq(
    distribution = qweibull,
    dparams = as.list(budget_weibull$estimate)
  ) +
  stat_qq_line(
    distribution = qweibull,
    dparams = as.list(budget_weibull$estimate)
  ) +
  labs(title = "Weibull")

qq_lognormal <- 
  ggplot(universal, aes(sample = budget)) +
  stat_qq(
    distribution = qlnorm,
    dparams = as.list(budget_lognormal$estimate)
  ) +
  stat_qq_line(
    distribution = qlnorm,
    dparams = as.list(budget_lognormal$estimate)
  ) +
  labs(title = "Log-normal")

qq_normal+ qq_exponential + qq_gamma + qq_weibull + qq_lognormal
```

The qq plot indicates normal and log normal are the worst fits as tails deviate the most from the reference line. The Exponential and Gamma model have the best fist as the right tail have the smallest distance from the reference line and most of the points overlap with the line.

```{r}
#fit AIC
AIC(
  budget_normal, 
  budget_exp, 
  budget_gamma, 
  budget_weibull,
  budget_lognormal
) |> 
  rownames_to_column(var = "model") |> 
  arrange(AIC) |> 
  gt()
```

The Gamma model has lowest AIC, which paired with the fitting of the qqplot, which suggests that it is the best at fitting budget data. 

###  Part 2: Downside Risk Analysis for Action Movie ROI

Action movies have been established as capital-intensive to produce, which can be proved as risky for budget investment in order to yield significant revenue. As a result, risk analysis into the bottom performing 25% movie ROI was performed across the entire film industry to model conservative target ROI to aim for, 

```{r}
action_roi <- data |> 
  filter(primary_genre == "Action", !is.na(roi)) |> 
  pull(roi) 

#observed ROI at 25% percentile
observed_q <- quantile(action_roi, 0.25) |> 
  round(3)

```
The observed 25% percentile of Action Movie ROI was `r observed_q`
```{r}
#Bootstrap Test
set.seed(5242)

bootstrap_results <- tibble(
  replicate = 1:1000
) |>
  mutate(
    boot_q = map_dbl(replicate, function(i) {
      action_boot <- sample(
        x = action_roi,
        size = length(action_roi),
        replace = TRUE
      )

      quantile(action_boot, probs = 0.25)
    })
  )

bootstrap_ci <- bootstrap_results |>
  summarise(
    lower = quantile(boot_q, probs = 0.025),
    upper = quantile(boot_q, probs = 0.975)
  )

#Method 2: SE multiplier
t_multiplier <- qt(0.975, df = length(action_roi) - 1)

bootstrap_se_ci <- bootstrap_results |>
  summarise(
    boot_se = sd(boot_q),
    lower = observed_q - t_multiplier * boot_se,
    upper = observed_q + t_multiplier * boot_se
  )

#Make into table
tibble(
  Calculation_method = c("Percentile bootstrap", "Bootstrap SE (t)"),
  Lower_Bound = c(
    bootstrap_ci$lower,
    bootstrap_se_ci$lower
  ),
  Upper_bound = c(
    bootstrap_ci$upper,
    bootstrap_se_ci$upper
  )
) |> 
  gt()
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| fig-align: center

#plot bootstrap
q3plot1 <- ggplot(bootstrap_results, aes(x = boot_q)) +
  geom_histogram(boundary = 0, binwidth = 0.025) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = observed_q,
    linewidth = 1,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = c(bootstrap_ci$lower, bootstrap_ci$upper),
    linewidth = 1
  )+
  labs(
    x = "Bootstrap in 25% quantiles",
    y = "Number of bootstrap samples",
    title = "Bootstrap distribution using Percentile Method",
    subtitle = "Dashed line shows the observed difference"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

q3plot2 <- ggplot(bootstrap_results, aes(x = boot_q)) +
  geom_histogram(boundary = 0, binwidth = 0.025) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = observed_q,
    linewidth = 1,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = c(bootstrap_se_ci$lower, bootstrap_se_ci$upper),
    linewidth = 1
  )+
  labs(
    x = "Bootstrap in 25% quantiles",
    y = "Number of bootstrap samples",
    title = "Bootstrap distribution using Standard Error Method",
    subtitle = "Dashed line shows the observed difference"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
q3plot1
q3plot2

```

```{r}
check <- tibble(
  method = c("Percentile bootstrap", "Bootstrap SE (t)"),
  gap_below = c(
    observed_q - bootstrap_ci$lower,
    observed_q - bootstrap_se_ci$lower
  ),
  gap_above = c(
    bootstrap_ci$upper - observed_q,
    bootstrap_se_ci$upper - observed_q
  ),
  width = c(
    bootstrap_ci$upper- bootstrap_ci$lower,
    bootstrap_se_ci$upper- bootstrap_se_ci$lower
  )
)

check |>  gt()
```

Both methods to calculate the confidence interval use the bootstrapped sample, which assumes the sample of Action films is representative of the population. Overall, the results were similar with the percentile interval (0.463, 0.679) and the standard error interval (0.460, 0.693) overlapping significantly. 

The percentile method does not consider symmetry as it takes the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles directly from the bootstrapped distribution, while the bootstrapped standard error method assumes the distribution is symmetric and approximately bell-shaped which places the lower and upper bounds equidistant from the observed 25th percentile (0.576). The Standard Error method slightly overstated the upper bound in comparison to the percentile bootstrap estimate while maintaining similar estimates for the lower bound. This may have been because the bootstrapped distribution is slightly left skewed where the percentile bootstrap method displays a larger gap between the observed estimate and the lower bound than the upper bound. The Standard error method also had a larger width in the confidence interval likely due to the larger tails, which increase the estimated Standard Error as a result. Since the percentile method does not rely on the symmetry assumption being accurate, it is best to use this method although both methods yielded similar results.

### Summary

Based on the analysis, it is recommended to select the Gamma distribution for the simulation. It had the best fit for the budget data as it matched the QQ-plot reference line the closest and had the lowest AIC value after evaluating five different models. It captured the right skew in budgets where few movie budgets had more expensive budgets compared to the majority of movies. 

In this sample, 25% of action films had an ROI of 0.576 or lower. We are 95% confident the true 25th percentile of the ROI for all action films across all studios lies between 0.463 and 0.679. For a conservative risk figure to plan around, Finance should consider 0.463 (46.3% return) for an underperforming Action film. 

## Task 4

```{r}

task4_data <- task_1_data |> 
mutate(
    flop = case_when(roi < 1 ~ "Flop",
                    TRUE ~ "Not flop"),
    flop = factor(flop, levels = c("Not flop", "Flop"))
  )
glimpse(task4_data)
```

The new flop variable only has two possible outcomes, which means it can be modeled by a Bernoulli distribution, where the parameter p measures the probability that a move is a flop. Hence, logistic regression is the appropriate choice as the log function $\log\left(\frac{p_i}{1 - p_i}\right)$ ensures the predicted probabilities remain between 0 and 1. The linear regression is not suitable as it assumes outcomes are continuous and normally distributed, while the flop variable only takes 0 and 1. Poisson regression is also not suitable as it is used when the outcome is a count with no upper limit. 

```{r, warning = FALSE}
library(brms)

```

```{r}
task4_data <- task4_data |> 
  filter(!is.na(cast_size), !is.na(primary_genre) ) |> 
  mutate(log_budget = log(budget)) |>
  mutate(across(c(log_budget, cast_size),
                ~ (.x - mean(.x)) / sd(.x),
                .names = "{.col}.z"))

freq_logistic_model <- glm(
  formula = flop ~ primary_genre + franchise_status + log_budget.z + cast_size.z,
  family = binomial,
  data = task4_data
)
summary(freq_logistic_model)
```
```{r, warning = FALSE}
confint(freq_logistic_model)

exp(coef(freq_logistic_model))
exp(confint(freq_logistic_model))

```
```{r}
#| fig.width: 12
#| fig.height: 12
check_model(freq_logistic_model)
```
Franchise orginal and cast size had little statistical st

The frequentist model reproduces the observed numbers of flops and non-flops. All VIFs are close to 1, which rules out colinearity. No individual film is overly influential. Most binned residuals fall within the error bounds, although some residuals around predicted probabilities of 20–30% fall were below the error interval. The homogeneity of variance and normality plots are not relevant for a binary outcome. We also assume the films are independent and that each numeric predictor has a linear relationship with the log-odds of a flop.
